entries.title: Hear the Correction, Not Just the Time

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Listen to this fictional message: Meet at the cafe at six. Sorry, I mean we're leaving from there at six. Come earlier if you want a drink.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Which reply fits if you don't want a drink? First: I'll arrive at six and order coffee. Second: I'll be outside before six, ready to leave.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: The second reply follows the corrected plan. Six is now the departure time. A drink is optional. Don't keep an early detail after the speaker has replaced it. Your answer should fit the current arrangement.

entries.prompt: Does the corrected six o'clock time mean arrive for coffee, or leave with the group?
entries.answer: Leave with the group. Be there before departure if you're joining them.

entries.title: An Excuse Can Sound Like Yes with a Problem
entries.hook: Did you decline, or ask for help?

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: My friends offered matching hoodies. I don't want one, so I said my size might not be available. Now they've found my size in three colours.

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: They heard a problem they could solve. Try naming your actual choice: Thanks for organising it. I'm going to pass on the hoodie, but I'm still coming to the evening.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: So I can decline the optional item without pretending I have a delivery problem?

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: Yes. Say which offer you're declining. That keeps the purchase separate from the invitation, and stops another helpful search for your size.

entries.prompt: Which is clearer: an invented obstacle, or your actual choice about the item?
entries.answer: Your actual choice. A solvable obstacle may sound like a yes waiting for help.

entries.title: Coming to Games Night Is Not Leading It
entries.hook: One yes became a different job.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Sam accepted a fictional games-night invitation. Later, the host asked him to explain the rules and lead the first round. He nearly wrote: Sure, happy to help. But he had only watched a short explanation of the game. He wasn't ready to lead a group.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Instead, he asked what the host needed. Then he replied: I can explain the opening example, but I don't know the rules well enough to run the whole game. Could somebody else lead the round?

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: He hasn't withdrawn his attendance. He's answered a new request honestly. Coming along, helping with one part and taking responsibility for the whole activity are different commitments.

entries.prompt: Did Sam refuse the invitation, or clarify the help he can offer?
entries.answer: He clarified the help he can offer. Agreeing to attend didn't automatically mean leading.

entries.title: Already Agreed? Have a Different Conversation
entries.hook: The earlier agreement changes your reply.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: I already told the organiser to order a hoodie for me. Now I don't want it. I'll write: I'm passing on the hoodie. Problem solved?

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: That sentence fits an optional offer you haven't accepted. Here, you've already agreed. Start with that: I know I asked you to order one. Is it still possible to change my answer?

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: And if the order has already gone through, I shouldn't pretend my new message erased the first agreement.

turns.speaker: Riley
turns.text: Right. Ask what's possible and discuss the next step. This fictional conversation doesn't decide anyone's refund rights. It shows why the same polite sentence doesn't fit every stage of an arrangement.

entries.prompt: Should Sam acknowledge his earlier yes before asking to change it?
entries.answer: Yes. Acknowledge what was agreed, then ask what can still be changed.
